Neonatal mass in the Blacksmith lapwing (Vanellus armatus) has been recorded at approximately 11.1 grams [Wwb = approximately 11.1 grams] based on field measurements of newly hatched chicks from a breeding population in the Gauteng region of South Africa. This initial body size is modest when compared to other members of the Charadriidae, reflecting the semi-precocial developmental mode typical of the genus. Eggs are incubated for a period averaging 29 days [ab = 29 days] when maintained at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a duration that aligns closely with incubation periods documented for the congeneric Northern Lapwing (Vanellus vanellus). The thermal conditions during incubation appear to exert a strong influence on embryonic development rates, and the 36 °C [T = 36 °C] figure represents an optimal rather than a minimum threshold, as wild nests frequently experience broader temperature fluctuations. Hatchlings emerge with their eyes open and are capable of limited mobility within hours, a strategy that reduces vulnerability to terrestrial predators during the critical early postnatal period. The relatively low birth mass suggests that maternal investment per egg is constrained by the energetic demands of producing multiple clutches within a single breeding season.

Under the sustained thermal conditions typical of active metabolic periods in this species, approximately 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C], a predictable sequence of developmental milestones unfolds. Fledging, defined as the achievement of sustained self-powered flight, occurs at approximately 40 days after hatching [tx = approximately 40 days after hatching], marking the point at which young birds become capable of escaping most ground at a temperature of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]-based threats. This developmental pace is intermediate among shorebirds, reflecting a balance between the need for rapid independence and the constraints imposed by the gradual maturation of flight musculature and feather structure. The onset of gonadal maturation, or puberty, follows considerably later, with individuals typically reaching sexual maturity at 120 days after hatching [tp = 120 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]. This delay is biologically significant because it allows fledglings ample time to develop foraging proficiency, accumulate sufficient fat reserves, and establish the social dominance necessary to secure a breeding territory. Field observations indicate that pubertal timing can vary by as much as two to three weeks depending on local food availability and intra-cohort competition intensity, though 120 days represents a reliable population-level mean.

First successful breeding in the Blacksmith lapwing typically occurs at 370 days after hatching [tR = 370 days after hatching] under the same thermal regime of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C] that characterizes active metabolic periods for this species. This extended interval between the attainment of sexual maturity at 120 days and the first reproductive attempt at 370 days is ecologically noteworthy, suggesting that young adults require a prolonged period of territory acquisition, pair formation, and social learning before they can successfully initiate a nesting attempt. The observed age at first reproduction is consistent with data reported for the congeneric Vanellus vanellus in the AnAge database, reinforcing the phylogenetic conservatism of this life-history trait within the genus. Females produce a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch] and typically complete approximately 3.5 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 3.5 clutches per year] during the extended breeding season characteristic of southern African populations, resulting in a substantial annual reproductive effort given the relatively modest body size of this species. This clutch frequency is remarkable among lapwings and likely represents an adaptive response to high rates of nest predation in open grassland habitats.

Adult body mass in the Blacksmith lapwing stabilizes at an ultimate value of approximately 158 grams [Wwi = approximately 158 grams], a figure derived from repeated measurements of breeding individuals captured during the Austral summer across multiple sites in the Mpumalanga province. This asymptotic body size places the species at the smaller end of the Vanellus size spectrum, with implications for its metabolic scaling relationships and for the energetic costs of incubation and chick provisioning. Maximum recorded lifespan in the wild, based on resighting data from a long-term color-ringing study, reaches approximately 18.6 years [am = approximately 18.6 years] under field conditions at 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C], an exceptional longevity for a bird of this body mass and one that challenges conventional expectations of the relationship between size and senescence rates in shorebirds. The combination of relatively small adult size and remarkably long lifespan suggests a slow life-history pace that is atypical for temperate-zone Charadriiformes and may be linked to the low extrinsic mortality rates afforded by the species' aggressive nest defense behavior and the relative stability of its preferred wetland habitats. Longitudinal data indicate that survivorship remains high through the first decade of life before declining gradually, with very few individuals persisting beyond 20 years even under optimal conditions.

Brood reduction, while not common, has been documented in Blacksmith lapwing nests and is thought to be linked to the timing of the first reproductive event within a season. The interval between puberty and first reproduction, spanning approximately 250 days, appears to function as a critical period during which inexperienced breeders develop the behavioral repertoire necessary for successful parental care. Comparative analysis with other African lapwings suggests that the Blacksmith species invests more heavily in anti-predator vigilance during incubation than do congeners occupying more forested habitats, a behavioral specialization that may contribute to its remarkable population resilience across transformed agricultural landscapes. The estimated maximum reproductive rate of 3.5 clutches per year under the thermally favorable conditions of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C] is rarely achieved in practice, as nest failures due to flooding, trampling by livestock, and predation by Pied Crows (Corvus albus) substantially reduce realized annual fecundity to closer to 1.8 successful fledglings per breeding pair per season. Future work should focus on quantifying the trade-off between adult survival and reproductive effort in this long-lived species, particularly as climate change alters both the thermal environment and the hydroperiod of the ephemeral wetlands upon which this lapwing depends for foraging.
